5 Superb Clarence Thomas Opinions To Mark His 35 Years At SCOTUS

The Federalist has compiled five of Thomas' greatest opinions to commemorate his 35 years on the nation's highest bench.

Actual Article Body:
The Federalist has compiled five of Thomas’ greatest opinions to commemorate his 35 years on the nation’s highest bench.

It may not be hard to believe, but Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas just hit yet another major career milestone.

The Bush 41 appointee marked 35 years on the high court on Friday, which comes months after he became the second-longest serving justice in U.S. history. Should he continue to serve through May 2028, Thomas would become the nation’s longest serving justice.

[READ: Leftists Tried To Stop Clarence Thomas From Going Further. They Failed Miserably]

Since joining SCOTUS, Thomas has authored numerous opinions upholding the Constitution and defending Americans’ God-given rights. And while there are too many to list in one article, The Federalist has compiled five of Thomas’ greatest writings to commemorate his 35 years on the nation’s highest bench.

The Second Amendment’s right to “keep and bear arms” is a core liberty guaranteed to all law-abiding Americans. And in Bruen, Thomas made sure New York’s gun-grabbers knew it.

Writing for the majority, Thomas upheld Americans’ right to carry firearms outside the home for purposes of self-defense. In doing so, he affirmed that the Second Amendment is not some “second-class right” to be trifled with, but one that garners equally as much value and respect as the others guaranteed by the Constitution.

“We know of no other constitutional right that an individual may exercise only after demonstrating to government officers some special need,” Thomas wrote. “That is not how the First Amendment works when it comes to unpopular speech or the free exercise of religion. It is not how the Sixth Amendment works when it comes to a defendant’s right to confront the witnesses against him. And it is not how the Second Amendment works when it comes to public carry for self-defense.”

[READ: The Best Lines From The Supreme Court’s Takedown Of New York’s Unconstitutional Gun Licensing Scheme]

Throughout his judicial career, Thomas has regularly championed the notion that all people, regardless of race, should be treated equally under the law. So, it wasn’t exactly surprising when the senior justice signed onto the Supreme Court’s Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard decision finding affirmative action policies to be unconstitutional.

Thomas also authored a concurring opinion in the case to drive home the point that affirmative action — which was devised to end discriminatory admissions decisions against black Americans — is now being used to discriminate against those who don’t check universities’ preferred diversity box (that is, white and Asian Americans). Trading discrimination for discrimination, he said, is completely untenable and wrong.

“Racialism simply cannot be undone by different or more racialism. Instead, the solution announced in the second founding is incorporated in our Constitution: that we are all equal, and should be treated equally before the law without regard to our race,” Thomas wrote. “Only that promise can allow us to look past our differing skin colors and identities and see each other for what we truly are: individuals with unique thoughts, perspectives, and goals, but with equal dignity and equal rights under the law.”

[READ: The 15 Best Zingers, Maxims, And Mic-Drops From Clarence Thomas’ Harvard Concurrence]

Thomas has never shied away from standing up for the little guy — especially when the law is on his side.

In Kelo v. New London, the Supreme Court upheld New London, Connecticut’s use of eminent domain to seize several homeowners’ private property to build a new Pfizer facility. The property owners alleged that the use of eminent domain violated the Fifth Amendment’s taking clause, which states that “private property [shall not] be taken for public use, without just compensation.” They more specifically reasoned that the seizure was unlawful because it was designed to benefit a private developer and not the general public.

In addition to joining the principal dissent, Thomas authored a solo dissent blasting the high court for “stray[ing]” from the clause’s “original meaning.” He further underscored the harmful impact the ruling would have on the nation’s poorest communities.

“Allowing the government to take property solely for public purposes is bad enough, but extending the concept of public purpose to encompass any economically beneficial goal guarantees that these losses will fall disproportionately on poor communities,” Thomas wrote. “Those communities are not only systematically less likely to put their lands to the highest and best social use, but are also the least politically powerful. If ever there were justification for intrusive judicial review of constitutional provisions that protect ‘discrete and insular minorities,’ … surely that principle would apply with great force to the powerless groups and individuals the Public Use Clause protects.”

Democrats often cite their preferred “experts” to justify their destructive policy decisions. This strategy was on full display in U.S. v. Skrmetti, in which the Biden administration sought to nullify a Tennessee law protecting kids from harmful “trans” procedures. Fortunately for America’s children, it’s one that Thomas and five of his colleagues weren’t buying.

While joining the majority opinion, the Bush 41 appointee authored a concurrence skewering the “expert class” and those who rely on its judgement to override what the law calls for.

“This case carries a simple lesson: In politically contentious debates over matters shrouded in scientific uncertainty, courts should not assume that self-described experts are correct,” Thomas wrote. “The Court today reserves ‘to the people, their elected representatives, and the democratic process’ the power to decide how best to address an area of medical uncertainty and extraordinary importance. … That sovereign prerogative does not bow to ‘major medical organizations.’ … ‘[E]xperts and elites have been wrong before — and they may prove to be wrong again.'”

[READ: In Landmark Skrmetti Case, Justice Thomas Demolishes The ‘Expert Class’]

It seems pretty ludicrous to suggest that the 14th Amendment — which was designed to ensure equal rights for freed slaves — bestows “birthplace citizenship” to the children of illegal aliens and foreign “birth tourists.” And yet, that’s what five justices held in Trump v. Barbara.

Thomas did not hold back on when it came to excoriating the Barbara majority’s decision. The senior justice penned a 91-page dissent going through the historical and legal record to demonstrate how devastatingly wrong the court’s holding is.

“I am not sure that today’s opinion will stand the test of time. The Citizenship Clause ‘added greatly to the dignity and glory of American citizenship.’ … Today’s opinion devalues that citizenship. I respectfully dissent,” Thomas concluded.

[READ: Thomas, Alito: In Birthplace Citizenship Ruling, John Roberts Imposes ‘Feudal’ ‘Darkness’]

Actual Article Body:
By FRANCINE WOLFISZ, NEWS REPORTER

Published:  08:39 AEDT, 28 October 2026   |  Updated:  08:39 AEDT, 28 October 2026

Thomas Markle's granddaughter said the child sex allegations he faces are 'not a surprise', adding that she always felt there was 'something off' about him.

Noelle Rasmussen, niece of Meghan Markle, made the astonishing claim just days after police in the Philippines revealed they were investigating the 82-year-old over allegations he had 'hundreds, if not thousands' of child sexual abuse images.

One of the photographs is alleged to show an image of Mr Markle having sex with an underage girl.

The Philippines' interior minister Jonvic Remulla said Mr Markle appeared to be 'a possible sex offender of the grossest kind'.

Mr Markle has denied any wrongdoing, admitting he paid for sex in the Philippines but insisting it was only with adult prostitutes.

His ex-wife Roslyn Loveless - and Ms Rasmussen's grandmother - is also understood to have sent a letter years earlier to the Metropolitan Police alleging he was a paedophile in January 2019, before its contents were passed on to Prince Harry and Meghan.

But it has since emerged that the Met Police reportedly misplaced the letter and failed to pass on the allegations to international agencies, including the FBI.

Ms Rasmussen, who recalled her late grandmother writing the letter, described the failure of Scotland Yard to pass on the allegations as 'embarrassing' and revealed she was not entirely surprised by the claims.

Noelle Rasmussen said the child sex allegations her grandfather Thomas Markle faces are 'not a surprise' and she always felt there was 'something off' about him

Mr Markle denies all of the allegations. Authorities in the Philippines are currently investigating

Speaking to The Telegraph, she said: 'Maybe it was a vibe that I subconsciously got… something's not right about a person, and you don't actively register it.

'But your body tells you when something's off.'

She added: 'The more and more I think about it, it just doesn't… I don't know why it's not a surprise.'

Ms Rasmussen added that she '100 per cent backs' the Duchess' decision to distance herself from her father.

However Ms Rasmussen's mother, Samantha Markle, has dismissed the claims.

Meghan's half-sister said previously that if her mother had sent the letter it was out of 'hatred and bitterness', and accused her of being an alcoholic and 'not credible'.

Mr Markle and Ms Loveless divorced in 1975, four years before he met Meghan's mother Doria Ragland.

It is understood that the Met is assessing whether to refer itself to a police watchdog over its handling of the letter.

Mr Markle's ex-wife Roslyn Loveless is understood to have sent a letter to the Met Police in 2019 accusing him of child sex abuse

In photos obtained exclusively by the Mail on Sunday, Mr Markle is seen in a Florida hospital after having his leg amputated earlier this year

Meghan Markle pictured in 2011 with her father Thomas who faces child sex abuse allegations

Meghan and her father have been estranged since at least 2018 when she married Prince Harry.

Their relationship broke down after he admitted staging paparazzi photos of himself prior to the wedding.

The Duchess wrote to him last December after his leg was amputated in the Philippines, allegedly telling him he posed a risk to children and would never be allowed to meet his grandchildren, Archie and Lilibet.

The Daily Mail has contacted the Metropolitan Police and Meghan Markle's representatives for comment.
